notes.title: 💫 Small Update, Big Impact: Controller Support & Audio Navigation!
notes.content:
Hey everyone!

We're excited to share a meaningful update today that takes us one big step closer to making our game more accessible to everyone. 🎮🧭✨


🕹️ Controller Support (With Rumble!)
You can now play the game using a controller! And yes — rumble feedback is fully supported. This isn’t just about comfort — it’s part of our mission to make the game more inclusive. Vibration cues will help signal key events or nearby points of interest, opening up new ways for players to engage with the world.


🔊 Audio-Based Object Detection
We've added directional audio cues to help players detect where objects of interest are located in relation to their character. If you're looking for something to collect, you'll now hear it — not just see it.



This feature is especially helpful for players with visual impairments, but we believe it will enrich the experience for all players. It's a step toward a game world that you can feel and hear, not just see.


🔄 Why This Matters
This might seem like a small update on the surface — but under the hood, this unlocks the ability to apply these systems consistently throughout the entire game. We can now expand this mechanism to guide players to NPCs, hazards, doors, and other interactive elements — all using audio and haptics.



There’s still work to do: consistent, clear audio design remains essential. But this update gives us the solid foundation we need to build a more intuitive and inclusive experience for everyone.



Thanks as always for your support — and a special shoutout to everyone in the accessibility community who continues to inspire us to do better. 💚



— Max
Dragonspirit Games

notes.title: UI Struggles, Second Screens & Accessibility – Dev Update for Gaia
notes.content:
Hey everyone,

Quick update from the Gaia development front — and a heartfelt thank-you as well!

A Second Screen (and a Generous Colleague)
I recently got a huge upgrade to my dev setup: a second monitor, thanks to the incredible generosity of one of my colleagues. It may sound small, but for a solo dev working on a game that’s deeply focused on accessibility, it’s a game-changer.

I can now work with the Unity editor on one screen while testing the game fullscreen on the other. It's massively improved my workflow — and made it much easier to focus on something I’ve been struggling with for a while:

UI Is Hard — Especially When It Needs to Work for Everyone
I’ve always known that UI design is tricky. But designing a user interface that works not just for sighted players, but also for players who are blind or have limited vision, is a whole different challenge.

Menus need to be fully keyboard-navigable. Focus needs to be clearly handled. Input has to be intuitive with a screen reader. And in a world where most games rely heavily on visual feedback, that’s… not easy.

Unity doesn’t always play nice with accessibility needs out of the box, so I’m working on:

Making all menus and buttons navigable via keyboard or controller

Giving audio feedback for every UI action

Planning to implement narrated menus for players using screen readers

It’s far from finished, but we’re making steady progress.

What's Next
Next, I’ll be tackling dropdowns, sliders, and other complex UI elements, making sure they’re usable without a mouse. It’s a big step forward in making Gaia one of the most accessible 2D platformers ever created.

Thank You
Thanks again to everyone following the journey of Gaia. Whether you’re here for the story, the accessibility focus, or just to see what’s possible in a solo dev game — I appreciate you.

If you have feedback, accessibility tips, or tools you love, I’m all ears.

Stay kind,
— Max (Dragonspirit Games)
